q245.question: How does The Urantia Book explain who actually built the Tower of Babel mentioned in the Bible, why they built it, and how it fell?
q245.answer:
The Urantia Book does not treat the Tower of Babel as a miracle story in which God scattered the languages. It explains it as an actual building project that the Nodites undertook after the fall of Dalamatia in order to preserve the glory of their race, and that was halted by internal strife over its purpose. The plan to build the tower was put forward by Bablot, a descendant of Nod, and from his name came the place name "Babel." [77:3.1, 77:3.3]

This event became the direct occasion for the dispersion of the Nodites, and it is counted as one of the causes of the long decline of Nodite culture that followed. [77:4.1] Below we look in turn at the background, the dispute over three purposes, the results, and the second attempt.

1. Background: A Plan to Preserve Racial Unity

After Dalamatia was submerged, the Nodites moved north and east and founded the new city of Dilmun. About fifty thousand years after the death of Nod, the offspring of the Prince's staff had become too numerous to live in the vicinity of Dilmun, and when intermarriage with the neighboring Andonite and Sangik tribes began, their leaders sought a way to preserve racial unity. A council of the tribes was called, and Bablot's plan was approved. [77:3.1]

Bablot proposed to erect a temple of racial glorification at the center of their territory, with a tower within it such as the world had never seen. This tower was to be "⟦Q 77:3.2⟧a monumental memorial to their passing greatness⟦/Q⟧." [77:3.2] Remembering the engulfment of Dalamatia, some insisted that it be built a safe distance from the sea. [77:3.2] Bablot hoped the new building would become the future center of Nodite culture and civilization, and its site later came to be known as Bablod and finally as Babel. [77:3.3]

2. Three Conflicting Purposes

After four and a half years of work, a great dispute arose over why the tower was being built, and all work stopped; when the news spread, many tribes gathered at the building site. [77:3.4] The three views were as follows.

The racial-memorial party: The largest group, almost half, wanted a dignified monument commemorating the history and racial superiority of the Nodites. [77:3.5]

The Dilmun-culture party: The second largest faction wanted the tower to commemorate the culture of Dilmun and hoped that Bablot would become a center of commerce, art, and manufacture. [77:3.6]

The worship party: The smallest group saw it as an opportunity to atone for the folly of their ancestors in joining the Caligastia rebellion, and proposed that "⟦Q 77:3.7⟧the tower should be devoted to the worship of the Father of all⟦/Q⟧" [77:3.7] and serve as the cultural and religious center taking the place of Dalamatia.

3. The Vote, the Fighting, and the Dispersion

The religious group was promptly voted down. The majority rejected the very teaching that their ancestors had rebelled, regarding it as a racial stigma. The remaining two views could not be settled by debate, and fighting broke out; the religionists, who were noncombatants, fled to the south, while the rest "⟦Q 77:3.8⟧fought until well-nigh obliterated⟦/Q⟧." [77:3.8]

This civil war greatly reduced the number of pure Nodites, and Nodite culture declined for more than one hundred and twenty thousand years, until the infusion of Adamic blood. [77:4.1] The Nodite centers established soon after the conflict also divided along the lines of this dispute. The remnants of the racial-memorial party went north and founded the northwestern Mesopotamian center that contributed to the later Assyrian stock, while those who had argued for culture and commerce moved east to Elam. [77:4.2-4.4]

4. The Second Attempt and Its Collapse

About twelve thousand years ago the Andites, the mixed race of Nodites and Adamites, undertook to raise a new temple on the ruins of the first structure, but the enterprise did not have sufficient support, and "⟦Q 77:3.9⟧it fell of its own pretentious weight⟦/Q⟧." [77:3.9] This region was long known as the land of Babel. [77:3.9]

To add a comparison from outside the book: Genesis 11 tells the story of the Tower of Babel as one of pride seeking to reach heaven and of the confusion of languages. The Urantia Book does not speak of a confusion of languages; it portrays the episode as an event in which racial pride and division of purpose destroyed a community.

Summary

The Tower of Babel was a tower the Nodites were building to Bablot's design in order to glorify their race; when the three purposes of racial memorial, cultural memorial, and worship collided, work stopped, and it ended in civil war and dispersion. [77:3.4-3.8, 77:4.1] The minority who wished to devote it to worship were rejected, and the later second attempt also collapsed. [77:3.9] This story shows how an enterprise that puts the glory of one's own group ahead of the worship of God divides itself.

q246.question: Was the "demon possession" of Jesus' time a real thing, and why does The Urantia Book say it can no longer happen today?
q246.answer:
The Urantia Book says that the demoniacal possession of the times before Jesus was not a mere figure of speech but something that really happened. The "demons" were the rebel midwayers who sided with Caligastia in the Lucifer rebellion, and before the universal coming of the Thought Adjusters they were able to influence the minds of certain inferior mortals. [77:7.1, 77:7.5] But after the Spirit of Truth was poured out upon all flesh at Pentecost, no disloyal spirit could ever again invade the human mind. [77:7.8]

1. Who Were the Rebel Midwayers?

The majority of the primary midwayers went into sin at the time of the Lucifer rebellion. Of the original 50,000, 40,119 joined the Caligastia secession. [77:7.1] The secondary midwayers originally numbered 1,984, and of these 873 failed to align themselves with the rule of Michael and were interned in connection with the planetary adjudication of Pentecost. [77:7.2] Both rebel groups are now held in detention awaiting the final adjudication of the system rebellion, but before the present dispensation they did many strange things on earth. [77:7.3]

Under certain circumstances they could reveal themselves to mortal eyes, especially the associates of Beelzebub, the leader of the apostate secondary midwayers. [77:7.4] The old writers called these rebel midwayers evil spirits and devils, and the apostate seraphim evil angels. [77:7.4]

2. How Was Demoniacal Possession Possible?

Before the coming of Christ Michael, that is, before the universal coming of the Thought Adjusters and the pouring out of the Master's spirit upon all flesh, the rebel midwayers were able to influence the minds of certain inferior mortals and somewhat control their actions. [77:7.5] The book explains that the method was similar to the way loyal midwayers function as contact guardians of the human minds of the reserve corps of destiny. [77:7.5]

This does not mean that every human being was exposed to such danger. "⟦Q 77:7.7⟧Even prior to Pentecost no rebel spirit could dominate a normal human mind⟦/Q⟧" [77:7.7]; the influence was limited to weak minds.

3. Jesus Distinguished Insanity from Demoniacal Possession

When the Gospels record that people brought to Jesus the sick, those possessed with devils, and the lunatics, this is not merely a figure of speech. [77:7.6] Jesus knew the difference between insanity and demoniacal possession, but in the minds of the people of that day the two conditions were greatly confused. [77:7.6] The Urantia Book also cautions us not to confuse these midwayers with the rebellious cherubim and seraphim who were on earth at the same time. [77:7.4]

4. Why Is It Impossible Since Pentecost?

Since the life of a Paradise bestowal Son, evil spirits can no longer indwell mortal minds on any world. [77:7.5] The entire group of rebel midwayers is held prisoner by order of the Most Highs of Edentia, and they no longer roam the world bent on mischief. [77:7.8] More fundamentally, "⟦Q 77:7.8⟧the pouring out of the Spirit of Truth upon all flesh forever made it impossible for disloyal spirits of any sort or description ever again to invade even the most feeble of human minds⟦/Q⟧." [77:7.8]

Therefore the stories of casting out devils since the arrival of the Spirit of Truth are the result of confounding a belief in demoniacal possession with hysteria, insanity, and feeble-mindedness. [77:7.7] At the same time the book keeps the balance by telling us not to imagine that such was not a reality in former ages. [77:7.7]

5. Midwayers Today and "Spiritualistic" Phenomena

The united midwayers now remaining on Urantia are loyal beings who work as the invisible associates of the reserve corps of destiny. [77:8.1, 77:8.13] It is clearly stated that they have nothing whatever to do with so-called "spiritualism" or mediumistic phenomena. [77:8.13]

Summary

Demoniacal possession was a real influence exerted by rebel midwayers upon weak human minds before Pentecost, but even then normal minds were not dominated. [77:7.5, 77:7.7] Through Michael's bestowal and the coming of the Spirit of Truth, all human minds were forever liberated from this possibility, and the rebel midwayers were imprisoned. [77:7.8] Therefore today's believer has no reason to fear evil spirits, and illnesses of the mind should be treated as illnesses.

q247.question: Did Noah's flood really happen? How does The Urantia Book explain the story of Noah and the great flood?
q247.answer:
The Urantia Book says that Noah was a real person and that there really were great floods in Mesopotamia, but that there has never been a universal flood covering the whole earth since life began. [78:7.4, 78:7.5] It explains that the Biblical story of Noah, the ark, and the flood was pieced together by Hebrew priests during the Babylonian captivity on the basis of memories of regional floods. [78:7.3, 78:7.4]

1. The Mesopotamian Floods That Really Happened

For the inhabitants of river valleys the annual floods were an ordinary part of life. [78:7.1] But for thousands of years after the submergence of the first Eden, the eastern coast of the Mediterranean and the mountains to the northwest and northeast of Mesopotamia kept rising, and about 5000 B.C. this elevation was greatly accelerated. The snows of the northern highlands greatly increased, causing unprecedented floods throughout the Euphrates valley each spring, and the inhabitants were driven to the highlands on the east. [78:7.2] For almost a thousand years scores of cities were practically deserted because of these floods. [78:7.2]

These floods completed the collapse of Andite civilization, and by the end of the flood period the second garden had ceased to exist. Traces of its former glory remained only in the south and among the Sumerians. [78:7.6]

2. Noah, a Real Person

"⟦Q 78:7.5⟧But Noah really lived⟦/Q⟧" [78:7.5]; he was a wine maker of Aram, a river settlement near Erech, and he kept a record of the river's rise from year to year. [78:7.5] He brought much ridicule upon himself by going up and down the valley advocating that houses be built of wood, boat fashion, and that the family animals be put on board each night during the flood season. [78:7.5]

Every year he warned the neighboring settlements that the floods would come within so many days. One year unusually heavy rainfall was added to the annual flood, so that the entire village was swept away; only Noah and his immediate family were saved in their houseboat. [78:7.5] This is the real kernel of the ark story.

3. How the Story Became a "World-wide Flood"

Almost five thousand years later, the Hebrew priests of the Babylonian captivity, trying to trace the genealogy of the Jewish people back to Adam, had great difficulty fitting the story together. One of these priests conceived the idea of having the whole world overwhelmed by water because of its wickedness, so as to connect Abraham with one of the three sons of Noah. [78:7.3] As a result, "⟦Q 78:7.4⟧L’histoire biblique de Noé, de l’arche et du déluge est une invention de la prêtrise hébraïque durant sa captivité à Babylone.⟦/Q⟧." [78:7.4]

The book also says that, since Mount Ararat was the sacred mountain of northern Mesopotamia and many traditions of this region were connected with the Babylonian flood stories, it is not surprising that Mount Ararat later became linked with the story of Noah. [77:4.12]

4. Universal Flood Legends and the Geological Facts

Many races harbor the story of a great flood covering the whole earth, but The Urantia Book says that there has never been a universal flood since life was established, and that the only time the surface of the earth was completely covered by water was during the Archeozoic ages, before the land had begun to appear. [78:7.4] Remains of ancient civilizations are found in and around Mesopotamia, but the traces of the still older Dalamatia lie under the waters of the Persian Gulf, and the first Eden is submerged beneath the eastern end of the Mediterranean. [78:7.7]

5. What We Can Learn from This Story

The Urantia Book deals elsewhere as well with the Hebrew priests' efforts to sanctify their national history. It says that when they rewrote history during the exile, they changed the secular history of their people into a fictitious and sacred history. [97:8.2, 97:8.7] The story of Noah is one example, showing that the stories of scripture should be read not literally but within the historical context in which they were produced.

Summary

From about 5000 B.C. there really were severe spring floods in Mesopotamia caused by the elevation of the highlands, and Noah, a wine maker near Erech, was a real person who built a houseboat and survived with his family. [78:7.2, 78:7.5] But there was no great flood covering the whole earth; the story of a world flood was created by the priests of the exile in order to connect the genealogies. [78:7.3-7.4]

q248.question: How does The Urantia Book use Singlangton's "One Truth" and ancestor veneration to explain why Chinese civilization long prospered and then stagnated?
q248.answer:
The Urantia Book says that the reason ancient Chinese civilization was for a time the most advanced large-scale civilization on earth lay largely in peace and unity and in a spiritual factor, the worship of the "One Truth" proclaimed by Singlangton. [79:6.8, 79:6.10] But it explains that when the longing to seek new truth turned into an attitude of venerating and preserving what was already known, what had been the world's most rapidly progressing civilization stagnated. [79:8.4]

1. Singlangton and the "One Truth"

Singlangton was the first among the yellow race to teach and lead his people to worship "One Truth" instead of many. [45:4.8] About one hundred thousand years ago, when he assumed the leadership of the tribes and proclaimed this worship, a brilliant era came to the yellow race. [64:6.15] Since the days of Singlangton the yellow race has been regarded as one of the most peaceful peoples on Urantia. [64:6.16] His teaching survived later in the concept of Shang-ti, the God of heaven. [94:5.3]

2. Four Factors That Put the Ancient Yellow Race Ahead

The book sums up the superiority of the ancient yellow race under four factors. [79:6.6]

Genetic: The northern Chinese were strengthened by the infusion of red and Andonite blood and later of Andite blood. [79:6.7]

Social: The yellow race learned early the value of peace among themselves, and from 25,000 to 5000 B.C. the highest large-scale civilization on Urantia was in central and northern China. [79:6.8]

Spiritual: "⟦Q 79:6.10⟧Long adherence to the worship of the One Truth proclaimed by Singlangton kept them ahead of most of the other races⟦/Q⟧." [79:6.10] While India languished, China forged ahead under the invigorating stimulus of a religion in which truth was enshrined as the supreme Deity, and this worship of truth stimulated research into the laws of nature and the potentials of mankind. [79:6.10-6.11]

Geographic: They were protected by mountains on the west and by the Pacific on the east. [79:6.12]

3. The Cause of Stagnation: From Exploration to Preservation

Awareness of past achievements, the conservatism of an agricultural population, and a well-developed family life gave rise to ancestor veneration, which finally culminated in the custom of honoring men of the past to the point of near worship. [79:8.3] Belief in the "One Truth" never entirely died out, but the search for higher truth became overshadowed by a tendency to venerate what was established. "⟦Q 79:8.4⟧Le génie de la race jaune se détourna lentement de la recherche de l’inconnu vers la préservation du connu.⟦/Q⟧." [79:8.4]

In addition, the cumbersome ideographic writing system limited the learned class, and social standardization and religious and philosophical dogmatization proceeded rapidly. Superstition increased, but a faint trace of the true concept of God was preserved in the imperial worship of Shang-ti. [79:8.7]

4. The Weakness and Strength of Ancestor Veneration

Weakness: Ancestor veneration promotes a backward-looking philosophy. The book says that it is folly to regard the past as the exclusive source of truth, for truth "⟦Q 79:8.8⟧lives always in the present, achieving new expression in each generation of men—even in each human life⟦/Q⟧." [79:8.8]

Strength: The value it places on the family. The remarkable stability and persistence of Chinese culture came from the supreme place given to the family, and filial devotion and family loyalty promoted the conservation of property, the sharing of experience between generations, the education of children, and a strong sense of duty and morality. [79:8.9-8.14] The book even says that the white race has never surpassed the Chinese in family loyalty, group ethics, and personal morality. [79:8.16]

5. A Civilization Awakening Again

This ancient culture has contributed much to human happiness, and although it long rested on the glories of its past, it is now said to be awakening to a new vision of the transcendent goals of mortal existence and once more taking up the struggle for unending progress. [79:8.17]

Summary

Chinese civilization long rose to the highest level in the world through peace, unity, and the spiritual vigor given by the worship of Singlangton's "One Truth." [79:6.8, 79:6.10] But as ancestor veneration made the past the source of truth, exploration turned into preservation, and the civilization stagnated. [79:8.4, 79:8.8] This lesson applies to personal faith as well: since truth is living and expanding, we should cherish what we have inherited while never ceasing to seek new truth.

q249.question: Who were the Cro-Magnons of archaeology according to The Urantia Book, and what was their relation to the Adamites?
q249.answer:
In The Urantia Book the Cro-Magnons are one of the blue men of Europe, one of the dozen or more groups of blue men that arose from the union of the migrating Adamites with the superior strains of the blue race. [80:1.7] Early European civilization was a blend of the vigor and artistry of the blue men with the creative imagination of the Adamites, and its art reached its height about fifteen thousand years ago. [80:3.3, 80:3.7]

1. Why Did the Adamites Unite with the Blue Men of Europe?

Adam's blood was shared with most of the races, but because the red and yellow men were far away and hard to reach, the Adamites, on leaving the Euphrates valley, naturally chose to unite with the blue men of Europe. [80:1.5] At that time the blue men had no religious practices that the Adamites would find objectionable, there was a strong attraction between the two races, and the best of the blue men considered it a great honor to mate with the Adamites. [80:1.6]

The migrating sons of Eden gradually united with the higher types of the blue race, invigorating their culture, and as a result they "⟦Q 80:1.7⟧produced a dozen or more virile and progressive groups of superior blue men, one of which you have denominated the Cro-Magnons⟦/Q⟧." [80:1.7] Because of these migration routes, the waves of early Mesopotamian culture flowed almost entirely into Europe, and this determined the origin of modern European civilization. [80:1.8]

2. The Life and Character of the Cro-Magnons

Honesty and chastity: The blue men were honest in all their dealings, free from the sexual corruption of the mixed Adamites, and they respected chastity. [80:3.4]

Education: They maintained an efficient system of child education in which both parents took part, and the children were taught the care of the caves, art, and flint making. [80:3.5]

Way of life: They were hunters, fishers, and food gatherers, expert boat builders, and builders of half-buried log huts. The southern Cro-Magnons for the most part lived in caves and grottoes. [80:3.6]

Art: They had courage, "⟦Q 80:3.7⟧but above all they were artists⟦/Q⟧" [80:3.7]. The Adamic mixture suddenly accelerated creative imagination, and the art of the blue man reached its height about fifteen thousand years ago. [80:3.7]

3. The Difficulty of Religion

On the other hand, the blue men also greatly lowered the cultural and spiritual level of the Adamites. Many of them were inclined to practice deceit, so that the Adamites found it very difficult to implant their religion in the Cro-Magnons, and for ten thousand years the religion of Europe remained at a very low level compared with that of India and Egypt. [80:3.3] This shows that the union of blood did not immediately guarantee spiritual transmission.

4. Climate Change, Decline, and Absorption into White Civilization

About fifteen thousand years ago, as the rain-bearing winds shifted northward, the great open grazing lands of Europe became covered with forests, and the hunters were driven to the river valleys and seashores, becoming herders, fishermen, and tillers of the soil. [80:3.8] This change brought cultural progress, but as slavery arose along with settled life, the whole Cro-Magnon type deteriorated. [80:3.9]

This retrogression continued until the final and en masse invasion of the Mesopotamians swept over Europe, "⟦Q 80:3.9⟧quickly absorbing the Cro-Magnon type and culture and initiating the civilization of the white races⟦/Q⟧." [80:3.9] When the Andite horsemen came across the Russian plains in the sixth and seventh millenniums before Christ, they blended with the blue men and became the ancestors of the Nordic race. [80:4.4-4.5]

Summary

The Cro-Magnons were one of the groups of blue men that arose from the union of Adamite migrants with superior blue men, and they excelled in honesty, chastity, education, and art. [80:1.7, 80:3.4-3.7] Religiously, however, they remained at a low level, and after the deterioration that followed the climate change they were absorbed by the final Andite invasion and became the foundation of white civilization. [80:3.3, 80:3.9] Behind their art, known through the cave paintings, stood the creative imagination of the children of Eden.

q250.question: What factors does The Urantia Book say are needed to preserve and advance today's civilization?
q250.answer:
The Urantia Book says that present-day civilization is the fruit of a long struggle since the days of Adam, and that because there is no longer any outside stimulus such as the Andites, the source of new culture, this civilization must be maintained and fostered. [81:6.1, 81:6.44] It then lists in turn the fifteen factors in which today's civilization is rooted, and concludes that only by preserving these essentials can man ensure the continued development and survival of civilization. [81:6.2, 81:6.43]

1. The Material Foundations: Environment, Capital, Science, Population

Natural environment: The nature and extent of a material civilization are largely determined by the available natural resources and by climate. [81:6.3]

Capital goods: "⟦Q 81:6.6⟧Culture is never developed under conditions of poverty⟦/Q⟧" [81:6.6]. A cultural civilization springs from material prosperity combined with leisure and ambition. Yet individual character of moral and spiritual value may be acquired without material wealth. [81:6.6]

Scientific knowledge: Science stabilizes philosophy by eliminating error and purifies religion by destroying superstition. [81:6.10]

Human resources: An increase of population up to a certain point is necessary, but beyond that line it brings self-destruction, and wise is the people that knows when to stop growing. [81:6.11-6.12]

2. Tools and Their Use: Efficiency, Language, Machines

The book names how wisely material resources are used, whether language is alive and growing, and how efficient mechanical devices are. [81:6.14, 81:6.16, 81:6.20] A common language promotes peace, insures culture, and augments happiness. [81:6.18] Machines free human labor for more worth-while tasks, but the transition problem of unemployment must be handled wisely, and "⟦Q 81:6.22⟧La science, guidée par la sagesse, peut devenir la grande libératrice sociale des hommes.⟦/Q⟧." [81:6.22]

3. What Matters Most: The Torchbearers and the Ideals

In handing on the torch of culture to the next generation, the home is always the basic institution, followed by play, social life, and the school. [81:6.23] Yet modern civilization has not developed an appreciation of ethics corresponding to its intellectual and scientific growth, and it "⟦Q 81:6.25⟧is at a standstill in spiritual development and the safeguarding of the home institution⟦/Q⟧." [81:6.25]

Racial ideals determine the destiny of the next generation. The home, church, and school of one generation predetermine the character trend of the next [81:6.26], and while intelligence controls the machinery of civilization and wisdom directs it, it is spiritual idealism that is the energy which lifts human culture to the next level. [81:6.27] The struggle of mankind will move from the struggle for existence to the struggle for a standard of living, and in the future to the struggle for quality of thinking. [81:6.28]

4. The Organization of Society: Co-ordination, Co-operation, Leadership

Co-ordination of specialists: As specialization increases, society without effective co-ordination grows weak and disintegrates. [81:6.29-6.30]

Placement in work: It is not enough to train people; they must be helped to find the right place, and no civilization can survive that long carries a large class of unemployed. [81:6.31-6.32]

The will to co-operate: The maintenance of world civilization depends on men learning how to live together in peace and fraternity. [81:6.36]

Leadership: Social co-operation depends on wise leadership, and the amount of such leadership has never exceeded one per cent of the population. [81:6.37, 81:6.42]

5. The Wisdom to Handle Change

Since society is not a divine institution but a phenomenon of progressive evolution, we should neither despise something because it is old nor accept something unconditionally because it is new. [81:6.39] Great social and economic changes should not be attempted suddenly; only moral and spiritual adjustments can be made on the spur of the moment. [81:6.40] The greatest danger is the collapse that may occur in passing from tried old methods to untried new ones. [81:6.41]

Summary

Civilization depends on material foundations such as environment, capital, science, and population; on the efficiency of language and machines; on co-ordination, co-operation, and leadership; and above all on the home and spiritual ideals. [81:6.2-6.42] The book says that "⟦Q 81:6.38⟧Les hautes civilisations naissent d’une liaison sagace entre la richesse matérielle, la grandeur intellectuelle, la valeur morale, l’habileté sociale et la clairvoyance cosmique.⟦/Q⟧." [81:6.38] For the believer this is a reminder that safeguarding the home and spiritual ideals is itself safeguarding civilization.

q251.question: The Urantia Book is said not to regard marriage as a sacrament joined by God. If so, what meaning do marriage and monogamy have?
q251.answer:
The Urantia Book regards marriage not as a sacrament made in heaven but as an institution that human society has evolved. Marriage which culminates in the home "⟦Q 83:8.1⟧is indeed man's most exalted institution, but it is essentially human⟦/Q⟧" [83:8.1], and the book says it should never have been called a sacrament. At the same time it highly esteems monogamous pair marriage as the eternal ideal of human sex evolution. [83:6.6]

1. Marriage Is an Evolved Social Institution

Mating is innate, and marriage is its evolutionary social repercussion. [82:1.1] Marriage is a device designed by society to regulate the relations arising from the fact of bisexuality, regulating personal sex relations as well as descent, inheritance, and social order. [83:1.1-1.3] While marriages may be approved or disapproved on high, "⟦Q 83:1.4⟧they are hardly made in heaven⟦/Q⟧." [83:1.4] Primitive marriage was chiefly industrial in nature, but as the mores of civilization advance it gradually becomes mutual, romantic, ethical, and idealistic. [83:1.5]

2. Why It Is Not a Sacrament

The Sethite priests made marriage a religious ritual, but for thousands of years after Eden mating remained a purely social and civil institution. [83:8.1] The book calls the likening of human associations to divine associations "most unfortunate," and says that marriage is a material function of the mortals of the evolutionary worlds. [83:8.2] Much spiritual progress may come through sincere effort within marriage, but since spiritual progress also comes through other avenues, this does not mean that marriage is sacred. [83:8.2]

Marriage cannot be compared with the relation of the Thought Adjuster to man, nor with the fraternity of Michael and his human brothers. [83:8.3] Moreover, the belief that marriage is consummated by divine action leads to the idea that marriage can under no circumstances be dissolved, but the book says that the very fact of the dissolution of marriages shows that Deity was not a party to the union. [83:8.4] It even names "⟦Q 83:6.3⟧the Christian error of regarding marriage as a sacrament⟦/Q⟧" [83:6.3] as one of the factors that fostered monogamy.

3. Why Monogamy Is Still the Ideal

Monogamy is unquestionably best for the children. [83:6.1] It is a cultural institution not natural to evolving man, but it was natural to the purer Nodites and Adamites and has been of great cultural value to all advanced races. [83:6.2] Monogamy is the yardstick that measures the advance of social civilization, and it promotes the fine sentiments, refinement of moral character, and spiritual growth that are impossible in plural marriage. [83:6.7] Pair marriage fosters the intimate understanding and co-operation that are best for parental happiness, child welfare, and social efficiency. [83:6.8]

Because this ideal entails self-denial, it so often fails when one or both parties are deficient in "⟦Q 83:6.6⟧that acme of all human virtues, rugged self-control⟦/Q⟧." [83:6.6] The book also urges that those who fail to secure a mate be treated kindly and considerately by the majority. [83:6.4-6.5]

4. The Ideal of Marriage on the Spheres on High

Although marriage is not a sacrament, there is an ideal of marriage on the spheres on high. On the capital of each local system the Material Sons and Daughters actually portray the ideal of the union of man and woman for the procreating and rearing of offspring. So the book says, "⟦Q 83:8.5⟧Après tout, le mariage idéal des mortels est humainement sacré.⟦/Q⟧." [83:8.5]

5. Advice to the Young

Marriage is the supreme dream of temporal ideality that man entertains. [83:8.6] Young people should be taught something of the realities of marriage, but their idealization of marriage should not be destroyed, for such dreams are a picture of the future goals of home life. [83:8.6-8.7] And the new companionate marriage must not go to the extreme of one partner monopolizing the personality and individuality of the other. [83:8.8]

Summary

Marriage is not a sacrament joined by heaven but the most exalted social institution that man has evolved. [83:1.4, 83:8.1] Yet monogamous pair marriage is an eternal ideal that, through self-control and self-denial, fosters fine sentiments and spiritual growth, and the ideal mortal marriage is "humanly sacred." [83:6.6-6.7, 83:8.5]

q252.question: What does ideal family life look like according to The Urantia Book, and what is the greatest danger threatening the home?
q252.answer:
The Urantia Book regards the home as man's supreme evolutionary acquirement and civilization's only hope of survival. [84:8.6] The ideal home is one in which parents fulfill their obligations, children grow up in love, and life is governed by brotherhood and co-operation, and good parents give their children the first revelation of the love of the Paradise parent. [84:7.26, 84:7.29-7.30] On the other hand, the book warns that the greatest danger threatening the home is "⟦Q 84:8.1⟧the menacing rising tide of self-gratification, the modern pleasure mania⟦/Q⟧." [84:8.1]

1. The Home Is the Foundation of Society

Marriage is "⟦Q 84:6.8⟧the mother of all human institutions⟦/Q⟧" [84:6.8], because it leads directly to home founding and home maintenance, and the home is the structural basis of society. When the home is good, society is good, and the great cultural stability of the Jewish and Chinese peoples lies in their strong family groups. [84:7.1] Marriage is now passing out of the stage in which the wife was regarded as property and into the personal era. [84:7.3]

2. The Relation of Parents and Children

The advancing ideal of family life lies in the recognition that bringing children into the world is not a right of the parents but entails the supreme responsibility of human existence. [84:7.25] Civilization holds that the parents assume all the duties and the child has all the rights. A child's respect grows not out of a sense of duty but as the result of the care, training, and affection shown in love, and true parents are engaged in continuous service. [84:7.26] The book also warns that attempts to shift parental responsibility to the state or the church will prove suicidal to civilization. [84:7.27]

3. The Fundamental Unit of Fraternity

The home is the arena in which children learn the ethics of blood brotherhood, and it is "⟦Q 84:7.28⟧the fundamental unit of fraternity⟦/Q⟧" [84:7.28] in which parents and children learn patience, altruism, tolerance, and forbearance. The book holds up as an example the Andite practice of the family council. Instead of patriarchal or autocratic rule, they discussed all family matters freely and frankly, and in such families the affection of parents and children grows together through fraternal devotion. [84:7.29]

4. The Spiritual Meaning of the Home

Family life is the progenitor of true morality, the ancestor of the consciousness of loyalty to duty. Living together forces adjustment to differing personalities, and so stabilizes and develops personality. [84:7.30] More than that, a good family reveals to the parents the attitude of the Creator toward his children, and true parents give their children the first of a long series of revelations of the love of the Paradise parent of all universe children. [84:7.30] The difference between the sexes, too, is not a cause for worry but a benefit, and man and woman will need each other even in the morontia and spirit careers. [84:6.5-6.6]

5. The Greatest Danger: The Pleasure Mania

In the past the chief motive for marriage was economic, but now all institutions are permeated by the pursuit of pleasure, so that marriage is sometimes regarded as a mere means of pleasure, and this has become the greatest threat to the home. [84:8.1-8.2] The book says that "⟦Q 84:8.4⟧the hunger of the soul cannot be satisfied with physical pleasures⟦/Q⟧" [84:8.4], and that even though one exhausts the resources of art, music, and adornment, one cannot thereby elevate the soul or nourish the spirit. [84:8.4]

This does not mean that enjoyment itself is condemned. Wholesome play, rest, and recreation have value, and man has earned the right to enjoy present-day joys. [84:8.5-8.6] But if self-gratification brings about the collapse of marriage and the destruction of the home, then such self-gratifications "⟦Q 84:8.6⟧have indeed cost a fatal price⟦/Q⟧" [84:8.6].

Summary

The ideal home is the place where, amid the responsible love of parents and fraternal co-operation, children learn morality and brotherhood and first experience the parental love of God. [84:7.25-7.30] The greatest enemy threatening that home is the unrestrained pursuit of pleasure, and the counsel of this paper is to enjoy life while looking well to the goal of destiny. [84:8.1, 84:8.6]

q253.question: If primitive religion began in fear and nature worship, was there no touch of God at all in that process?
q253.answer:
The Urantia Book states clearly that primitive religion was a product of natural evolution, growing out of human fears and illusions and nature worship without revelation. [85:0.1, 86:0.1] But that process was not unrelated to God. The sixth adjutant spirit (the spirit of worship) and the seventh adjutant spirit (the spirit of wisdom), part of the cosmic mind, were operating in primitive minds from the beginning, and primitive religion prepared the soil of the mind for the Thought Adjuster that was to come later. [85:7.1, 85:7.3, 86:7.6]

1. Primitive Religion Born of Fear and Illusion

The book says, "⟦Q 85:0.1⟧Les animaux supérieurs ont des peurs, mais pas d’illusions, donc pas de religion.⟦/Q⟧." [85:0.1] Man created primitive religion through fear and illusion. Primitive man worshiped every natural phenomenon he could not understand, and forces such as storms, floods, earthquakes, and fire made a deep impression on his mind. [85:0.4]

The objects of worship widened step by step. The first object to be worshiped by evolving man was a stone, followed by hill worship [85:1.1, 85:1.5], and then plants and trees, animals, the elements, the sun, moon, and stars, and finally man himself. [85:2.3, 85:3.2, 85:4.1, 85:5.1, 85:6.1]

2. The Fear of Chance and Bad Luck

Another origin of evolutionary religion was the experience of good and bad luck. [86:1.1] For primitive man struggling for survival, the fear of unseen calamity overshadowed every joy. [86:1.2] When he could not find the material causes of his sufferings, he moved toward spirit explanations. [86:2.2] Primitive religion was a kind of insurance premium against the perils of the forest. [86:7.1]

3. The Spirit of Worship and the Spirit of Wisdom

Yet all this time the sixth adjutant spirit was operating in primitive minds, constantly stimulating the worship urge. Although animal fear motivated worship and worship became centered on objects of nature, the spirit of worship "⟦Q 85:7.1⟧gave definite origin to the human impulse to worship⟦/Q⟧" [85:7.1]. The earliest worship, activated by the adjutant mind-spirit, was functioning long before man was able to respond fully to spiritual influences. [85:2.6]

Only when the worship urge is guided by wisdom does it develop into real religion. When the seventh adjutant, the spirit of wisdom, ministers effectively, man begins to turn away from the objects of nature "⟦Q 85:7.3⟧to the God of nature and to the eternal Creator of all things natural⟦/Q⟧." [85:7.3] We should also remember that in the primitive mind there was little distinction between fearing and worshiping. [85:7.2]

4. Evolutionary Religion and Revelatory Religion

Unaided evolution never originated gods higher than the glorified spirits of deceased humans. [85:6.3] The book draws this contrast: "⟦Q 85:6.3⟧La religion évolutionnaire crée ses dieux à l’image et à la ressemblance de l’homme mortel ; la religion révélée cherche à faire évoluer les mortels et à les transformer à l’image et à la ressemblance de Dieu.⟦/Q⟧." [85:6.3]

5. Preparation for the Thought Adjuster

Primitive religion started from mistaken concepts, but it did its work. It kept man from falling into fatalism or despair and impressed upon him that he must regulate his conduct and that there is a supermaterial world. [86:7.3, 86:7.5] Above all, primitive religion prepared the soil of the human mind, by the force of false fear, for the bestowal of the Thought Adjuster, and the Adjusters have ever since labored unceasingly to transmute the fear of God into love. [86:7.6]

Summary

Primitive religion is a natural product that grew out of fear, illusion, and anxiety about chance [85:0.1, 86:1.1], but underlying it from the beginning were the adjutant spirits of worship and wisdom. [85:7.1-7.3] And that age of fear became the preparation for receiving the Thought Adjuster. "⟦Q 86:7.6⟧L’évolution est peut-être lente, mais elle est infailliblement efficace.⟦/Q⟧." [86:7.6]

q254.question: Are religious rituals and symbols (the cult) truly necessary for the spiritual life? Please explain the conditions The Urantia Book gives for a desirable new cult.
q254.answer:
The Urantia Book judges that the cult (ritual and symbol) is useful for preserving and stimulating moral sentiments and religious loyalty, but that it has at the same time been the greatest obstacle to social reconstruction and spiritual progress. [87:7.1-7.2] In conclusion it says that the cult is the "skeleton" around which true religion grows, and that living personal spiritual experience must be its body. [87:7.10] It also stresses that when the religion of Jesus is restated, a new symbolism must be developed. [87:7.6]

1. The Roots of the Cult: The Ghost Cult

Primitive religious ritual arose from anxiety about bad luck and an excessive fear of the dead, and was mostly negative in character, seeking to avoid, expel, or coerce ghosts. [87:0.1] It was merely insurance against calamity, not an investment for a higher future. [87:0.1] Even so, this fear led mankind onto the path of religious evolution, and human imagination will not cast anchor until it reaches the concept of the true God. [87:0.2]

2. Why the Cult Has Persisted, and Its Dangers

The cult has persisted because it provided a symbolism that preserved and stimulated moral sentiments and religious loyalty. Every inspiring ideal seeks a symbol to perpetuate itself. [87:7.1] But the more the ceremonies grew unconsciously, the more strongly they held their devotees, and the cult, while satisfying the emotions, retarded progress. [87:7.2] "⟦Q 87:7.5⟧A meaningless cult vitiates religion when it attempts to supplant philosophy and to enslave reason⟦/Q⟧" [87:7.5].

3. Modern Believers Who Need Symbols

At the same time the book regrets that so many modern believers in moral standards and spiritual ideals have no adequate symbolism, no cult of mutual support, nothing to belong to. But a religious cult cannot be manufactured; "it must grow" [87:7.3]. The early Christian cult was the most effective and enduring ritual, but it lost its vitality as its fundamental doctrines collapsed in the scientific age. [87:7.4]

4. The Conditions of a New Cult

The conditions for a new cult that the book presents are as follows.

Foundation: It must be founded on the concept of the fatherhood of God and embrace the ideal of the brotherhood of man. [87:7.6]

Starting point: The old cults were too egocentric; "⟦Q 87:7.7⟧the new must be the outgrowth of applied love⟦/Q⟧" [87:7.7].

Goals: It must not stop at fostering sentiment and promoting loyalty, but must facilitate spiritual progress, enhance cosmic meanings, augment moral values, encourage social development, and stimulate a high type of personal religious living, providing goals that are both temporal and eternal. [87:7.7]

Home: It cannot survive unless it is founded on the biologic, sociologic, and religious importance of the home. [87:7.8]

Mystery and personal character: It must embrace a worth-while but not wholly attainable mystery, and it must be something the individual practices voluntarily yet can also share with others. [87:7.9]

Simplicity and dynamism: It will not function if it is too complex, and it must be dynamic, not static. [87:7.9-7.10]

5. Lessons for the Life of Faith

Believers must take care that ceremonies do not harden into rigid, enslaving fixed rituals. A cult can never survive if it retards moral growth and fails to foster spiritual progress. [87:7.10] When truth was abundant and the cult was elastic, truth grew rapidly and expanded freely. [87:7.5]

Summary

The cult has value as a symbol that preserves sentiment and loyalty, but when it hardens it blocks progress. [87:7.1-7.2] A desirable new cult must be founded on the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man, grow out of applied love, and be simple and dynamic. [87:7.6-7.10] And all such symbols are only the skeleton that holds the living spiritual experience of the individual. [87:7.10]

q255.question: What does The Urantia Book mean when it says that venerating scripture too highly can also become "fetishism"?
q255.answer:
In The Urantia Book a fetish is an object that is feared or worshiped because a spirit or a mysterious power is believed to dwell in it. The book explains that fetish worship began with stones and animals and moved on to relics, images, and finally to "words," and it says, "⟦Q 88:2.6⟧Words eventually became fetishes, more especially those which were regarded as God's words⟦/Q⟧" [88:2.6]. This does not mean that scripture itself is bad; it means that the attitude which regards scripture as the sole vessel of truth and so imprisons spiritual imagination and reason is a refined form of primitive fetishism.

1. The Origin of Fetishes

Primitive man tried to make fetishes of anything unusual, and chance was the origin of many fetishes. [88:1.1] The first fetishes were stones with peculiar markings, and later trees, animals, certain days and numbers, and even parts of the body became fetishes. [88:1.2-1.8] Extraordinary persons too were regarded as fetish personalities and were revered as holy and infallible. [88:1.10]

2. Fetishes Carried On in Relics, Images, and Shrines

Ghosts were believed to like to dwell in the objects they had possessed during life, and this belief explains the efficacy of modern relics. [88:2.1] The book says that "⟦Q 88:2.2⟧the relics of modern religions represent an attempt to rationalize the fetish of the savage⟦/Q⟧" and so to give it a place of dignity. [88:2.2] Idols were a refined form of fetishism. [88:2.4] Moses tried to check fetish worship through the second commandment against graven images, but he wisely did not suddenly destroy the old fetishes. [88:2.5]

3. When Words and Scripture Become Fetishes

Yet in this way "⟦Q 88:2.6⟧the sacred books of many religions have become fetishistic prisons incarcerating the spiritual imagination of man⟦/Q⟧." [88:2.6] Even Moses' effort against fetishes became a supreme fetish and was used to stultify art. [88:2.6] The fetish words of authority were fear-producing doctrines, and doctrinal fetishes deliver men over to bigotry, fanaticism, superstition, intolerance, and cruelty. [88:2.7]

The book gives these concrete examples.

Believing that all truth is in the book: If one believes not only that what is in a sacred book is true but that all truth is contained in it, then if the book says the earth is flat, people will refuse to accept even clear evidence. [88:2.7]

Deciding by a chance passage: Opening a sacred book at random and taking the passage that catches the eye as a guide for life decisions "⟦Q 88:2.8⟧is nothing more nor less than arrant fetishism⟦/Q⟧." [88:2.8]

Swearing with a hand on the book: This too is a form of refined fetishism. [88:2.8]

4. Still, Progress Is Progress

At the same time the book keeps the balance. To advance from fearing the fingernail trimmings of a chief to adoring a superb collection of letters, laws, legends, poems, and chronicles represents "real evolutionary progress," and such a collection reflects the winnowed moral wisdom of many centuries. [88:2.9] It also says that modern respect for wisdom and truth is the result of moving away from the fetish-making tendency toward higher thinking. [88:2.7] But it points out as well that when writings came to be regarded as divinely inspired, their authority soon led to the establishment of church authority. [88:2.10]

5. Magic and Science, and Our Task

Magic, which grew up alongside fetishes, was a branch that reached out from the tree of evolutionary religion and bore the fruit of science. [88:6.5] Ancient magic was "⟦Q 88:6.8⟧the cocoon of modern science⟦/Q⟧," but it is now no longer useful. [88:6.8] The book warns that if modern education fails, people may quickly revert to primitive beliefs in magic. [88:6.7]

Summary

Fetishism is the attitude of fearing and worshiping objects or words because a mysterious power is thought to dwell in them, and scripture too becomes a fetish when it is revered as an infallible object containing all truth or used as an instrument of divination. [88:2.6-2.8] To respect the moral wisdom contained in scripture is progress [88:2.9], but the point of this teaching is that, since living truth keeps growing outside the book as well, we should not imprison our spiritual imagination and reason within the book.

q256.question: How does The Urantia Book see the ideas of sin, sacrifice, and atonement as having arisen, and how does it ask us to understand sin and forgiveness today?
q256.answer:
The Urantia Book explains that the ideas of sin, sacrifice, and atonement evolved before revealed religion out of taboo and fear and out of the primitive notion of a "debt" owed to the gods. [89:2.2, 89:4.5-4.6] For modern man it redefines sin as "⟦Q 89:10.2⟧deliberate disloyalty to Deity⟦/Q⟧" [89:10.2], and says that God's forgiveness is not something to be purchased but only to be received as the consciousness that the loyalty relation has been renewed. [89:10.6]

1. From Taboo to Sin

The fear of chance and bad luck gave birth to primitive religion, and religion developed from magic and ghosts through spirits and fetishes to taboos. [89:2.1] When men came to imagine good and bad spirits and taboos received the sanction of religion, the concept of sin appeared, and it was universally established before revealed religion came. [89:2.2] To primitive man, "⟦Q 89:2.3⟧Le péché était rituel, et non rationnel ; un acte et non une pensée.⟦/Q⟧." [89:2.3] Violation of a taboo was both a crime and a sin, and calamities of the community were regarded as punishment for tribal sin. [89:2.4]

2. Renunciation and Humiliation

In the next stage came fasting, the renunciation of pleasure, the seeking of poverty, and bodily mortification. [89:3.1-3.4] By these methods men sought to accumulate extra credit in the ledgers of the gods. [89:3.5] The book judges, "⟦Q 89:3.7⟧La maitrise de soi est une meilleure politique humaine pour régler sa conduite que l’extrême reniement de soi.⟦/Q⟧." [89:3.7]

3. The Formation of the Ideas of Sacrifice and Atonement

There were sacrifices of gift and thanksgiving and sacrifices of debt and redemption, and later the concept of substitution developed. [89:4.2] As the traditions of the Planetary Prince and of Adam were handed down, the concepts of sin and original sin spread, and the doctrine of original sin or racial guilt made every person start out in serious debt to the spirit powers. [89:4.5-4.6] Later sacrifice was combined with the concept of the covenant, which stabilized religion, but early sacrifice was not a free gift of thanksgiving; it was bargaining to purchase prosperity and not an expression of true worship. [89:8.4, 89:8.6]

4. From Sacrifice to Sacrament

Sacrificial rites gradually rose to the symbolic level and developed into sacraments. [89:9.1, 89:9.4] Paul may have burdened Christianity unnecessarily with his teaching of blood and sacrifice, but he made an end once and for all of the doctrine of redemption through human or animal sacrifices. According to him, Christ became the final and complete sacrifice. [89:9.3] The book says that this compromise shows that even revelation must conform to the gradual control of evolution. [89:9.3]

5. Sin and Forgiveness for Modern Man

The men of old could become conscious of God's favor only through sacrifice, but modern man must develop new techniques for achieving the self-consciousness of salvation. [89:10.1] The book sums it up as follows.

Sin redefined: Sin is deliberate disloyalty to Deity, and there are degrees: the partial loyalty of indecision, the divided loyalty of confliction, the dying loyalty of indifference, and the death of loyalty exhibited in devotion to godless ideals. [89:10.2]

Guilt distinguished from sin: The sense of guilt is the consciousness of having violated the mores, but it is not necessarily sin; without conscious disloyalty there is no real sin. [89:10.3]

The positive meaning of the sense of guilt: The ability to feel guilt is not a mark that brands man as base but a sign that distinguishes him as a creature of potential greatness, the first stimulus that leads on to the conquests of faith. [89:10.4]

Confession: Confession does not remove the consequences in time and space, but it is essential to religious growth. [89:10.5]

Forgiveness: Forgiveness is the renewal of broken loyalty relations, and "⟦Q 89:10.6⟧the forgiveness does not have to be sought⟦/Q⟧" [89:10.6], only received as the consciousness that the relation has been re-established.

Summary

The ideas of sin, sacrifice, and atonement evolved from primitive notions of taboo, fear, and a debt owed to the gods, and sacrifice gradually turned into sacrament. [89:2.2, 89:4.6, 89:9.4] The Urantia Book asks us to understand sin as deliberate disloyalty to God and forgiveness as the restoration of the loyalty relation. [89:10.2, 89:10.6] Therefore the believer need not strive to pay a price, but simply return in loyalty to God and go forward joyfully.

q257.question: If prayer cannot change God, why should we pray, and what are the conditions of effective prayer?
q257.answer:
The Urantia Book says that prayer is not a means of turning God's mind in order to get what we want, but an effort to adjust the human personality to the will of God. "⟦Q 91:8.2⟧La magie fut une tentative pour adapter la Déité aux circonstances ; la prière est l’effort pour adapter la personnalité à la volonté de la Déité.⟦/Q⟧." [91:8.2] Prayer does not change God, but it works great and lasting changes in the one who prays, and God answers with ever larger revelations of truth, beauty, and goodness. [91:4.5, 91:8.11]

1. Why Is Prayer Necessary?

Real prayer attains reality. The book uses this image: "⟦Q 91:8.9⟧Même quand les courants aériens sont ascendants, nul oiseau ne peut prendre son essor sans déployer ses ailes.⟦/Q⟧." [91:8.9] Prayer is a technique of using the ascending spiritual currents of the universe; it augments spiritual growth, modifies attitudes, and yields the satisfaction that comes from communion with divinity. [91:8.9-8.10] Prayer is a subjective act, yet it contacts mighty objective realities, and it is the most potent stimulus to spiritual growth. [91:8.11]

Prayer has fostered in evolving mankind peace of mind, cheerfulness, calmness, courage, self-mastery, and fair-mindedness. [91:4.5] And sincere prayer of faith is a mighty force for the promotion of personal happiness, individual self-control, social harmony, moral progress, and spiritual attainment. [91:6.3]

2. The Limits of Prayer

Prayer cannot directly affect the physical environment unless it is linked with the will of the spiritual forces and the material supervisors. [91:6.1] Prayer is not a technique for curing real organic disease, but it has contributed greatly to the cure of mental and emotional illness and has enhanced the effect of other treatments. [91:6.2] So the book says, "⟦Q 91:6.5⟧Do not be so slothful as to ask God to solve your difficulties⟦/Q⟧" [91:6.5], and urges us instead to ask for wisdom and spiritual strength while we grapple with our problems.

3. Ethical Prayer

Prayer that seeks selfish advantage over one's fellows cannot be ethical, and such prayer degenerates into pseudo magic. [91:4.1] Prayer must never become a substitute for action; all ethical prayer is a stimulus to action. [91:4.2] We must be fair in prayer and not expect God to love us more than our friends, neighbors, or even enemies. [91:4.3] "⟦Q 91:8.13⟧Ne priez que pour des valeurs, non pour des choses ; pour la croissance, et non pour la satisfaction.⟦/Q⟧." [91:8.13]

4. Conversation with the Indwelling Adjuster

Prayer began as primitive man's conversation with an imagined "other self" and was finally sublimated into true communion with the Paradise Father. [91:3.3-3.4] As the most effective technique for practical purposes, the book says that we should recognize the truth that this other self is now God indwelling us in the factual presence of the Adjuster, so that we "⟦Q 91:3.7⟧can talk face to face, as it were⟦/Q⟧" [91:3.7], with him. God answers the soul's attitude, not the words. [91:8.12]

5. Seven Conditions of Effective Prayer

The book gives seven laws of successful petitioning. [91:9.1]

First, cosmic stamina that sincerely and courageously meets the problems of universe reality. [91:9.2]

Second, the diligence that honestly exhausts every possibility of human adjustment. [91:9.3]

Third, surrendering the wishes of mind and the cravings of soul to the transforming embrace of spiritual growth. [91:9.4]

Fourth, a wholehearted choice of the divine will, without indecision. [91:9.5]

Fifth, unreserved dedication to the actual doing of the Father's will. [91:9.6]

Sixth, concentrating on seeking divine wisdom to solve the specific problems met in the Paradise ascension. [91:9.7]

Seventh, having "faith—living faith" [91:9.8].

Summary

Prayer is not an art of persuading God but an effort to adjust oneself to the will of God, and as a result the one who prays is changed and grows. [91:8.2, 91:4.5] Effective prayer has as its conditions courage and diligence, the choosing and doing of the divine will, the seeking of wisdom for the ascent, and living faith. [91:9.2-9.8] It is worth remembering the saying that only a spiritual child would try to change God. [91:8.8]

q258.question: What are the five "epochal revelations" spoken of in The Urantia Book, and what is the relation between evolutionary religion and revealed religion?
q258.answer:
The Urantia Book says that there have been many religious revelations on Urantia, but only five of epochal significance: the Dalamatian teachings, the Edenic teachings, Melchizedek of Salem, Jesus of Nazareth, and the Urantia Papers. [92:4.4-4.9] Revelation does not abandon evolutionary religion; it sorts, censors, and uplifts it, and so it always keeps in touch with evolution, adapted to man's capacity of receptivity. [92:4.1]

1. The Relation between Evolutionary Religion and Revealed Religion

Evolutionary religion is an emotional reaction born of the realization and fear of the unknown, while revealed religion is the response of the real spiritual world to the human hunger to believe in and depend upon the Deities. "⟦Q 92:4.3⟧La religion évolutionnaire décrit les tâtonnements de l’humanité qui tourne en rond à la recherche de la vérité ; la religion révélée est cette vérité même.⟦/Q⟧." [92:4.3] Revealed religion is always characterized by belief in a Deity of final value and by the concept of the survival of personal identity after death. [92:4.2]

But "⟦Q 92:4.1⟧revelation is evolutionary but always progressive⟦/Q⟧" [92:4.1]. If revelation is to exalt evolutionary religion, it must not be too far removed from the thought of its age, so religion by revelation is always limited by man's capacity of receptivity. [92:4.1]

2. The First Revelation: The Dalamatian Teachings

The true concept of the First Source and Center was first proclaimed by the one hundred corporeal members of the staff of Caligastia, the Planetary Prince. This revelation continued for more than three hundred thousand years but was abruptly terminated by the planetary rebellion and the disruption of the teaching regime. [92:4.5] Except for the work of Van, its influence was practically lost, and the red men retained it longest. [92:4.5]

3. The Second Revelation: The Edenic Teachings

Adam and Eve again presented the concept of the Father of all to the evolutionary peoples, but the disruption of the first Eden halted the revelation before it had fully begun. Their teachings were carried on by the Sethite priests and changed the course of religious evolution in the Levant, but by 2500 B.C. mankind had largely lost sight of them. [92:4.6]

4. The Third Revelation: Melchizedek of Salem

Melchizedek, the emergency Son of Nebadon, made trust and faith his basic precepts, teaching men to trust in the almighty beneficence of God, and proclaimed that faith was the act by which men earned God's favor. [92:4.7] His teachings became mingled with various evolutionary religions and developed into the theologic systems of the first millennium after Christ. [92:4.7]

5. The Fourth and Fifth Revelations: Jesus and the Urantia Papers

Christ Michael revealed God as the Universal Father, and the substance of his teaching was love and service: the voluntary worship of love that responds to the Father's love, and the freewill service bestowed upon one's brothers. [92:4.8]

The Urantia Papers are the most recent presentation of truth, and they differ from previous revelations in that they are not the work of a single personality but a composite presentation by many beings. [92:4.9] The book frankly states of itself that "⟦Q 92:4.9⟧no revelation short of the attainment of the Universal Father can ever be complete⟦/Q⟧" [92:4.9], acknowledging that all celestial ministrations are partial and transient.

6. Revelation and Religious Leaders

The concept of God has been formed by a blending of the pre-existing ideas of the evolutionary cults, the sublime ideals of revealed religion, and the viewpoints of the great religious leaders. [92:5.1-5.4] The leaders often became objects of superstitious awe, but they were the fulcrum on which the lever of revealed truth rested. [92:5.7]

Summary

The five epochal revelations are Dalamatia, Eden, Melchizedek, Jesus, and the Urantia Papers, and each in its age enlarged the truth that makes God known as Father. [92:4.4-4.9] Revelation does not so much replace evolutionary religion as purify and uplift it, and it is given progressively within man's capacity of receptivity. [92:4.1] The fact that even The Urantia Book says it is not complete teaches an attitude of humble inquiry. [92:4.9]

q259.question: Who, according to The Urantia Book, is Melchizedek, the king of Salem who appears briefly in Genesis, what did he teach, and where is he now?
q259.answer:
In The Urantia Book, Melchizedek of Salem is Machiventa Melchizedek, an "emergency Son," one of the twelve planetary receivers of Urantia, who volunteered and was incarnated in the temporary likeness of a human being. [93:1.3] He appeared 1,973 years before the birth of Jesus and for ninety-four years taught at Salem the one God and salvation by faith; this was the third epochal revelation to Urantia. [93:2.1, 93:4.16, 92:4.7]

1. Why Did He Come?

For thousands of years after the failure of the Adamic mission, revealed truth was in danger of extinction, and by about 3000 B.C. the concept of God had grown very dim. [93:1.1] The twelve Melchizedek planetary receivers petitioned the Most Highs of Edentia for help but were told to solve the problem themselves, and Machiventa volunteered to do what had been done only six times in all the history of Nebadon: to personalize as a temporary man and bestow himself as an emergency Son. [93:1.2-1.3]

2. What Kind of Being Did He Live As?

He first made his appearance at the tent of Amdon, a Chaldean herder of Sumerian extraction, and soon became known as the priest of El Elyon and the sage of Salem. [93:2.1, 93:2.4] He never married and could not have left offspring; his body was a special physical body like those used by the corporeal staff of Caligastia. [93:2.6] He received a Thought Adjuster, and through this experience the Adjuster gained a practical introduction to the later indwelling of Michael. [93:2.7]

3. What Did He Teach?

The creed of Salem was very simple: to believe in El Elyon, the one Universal Father of all things; to accept the covenant with the Most High, "⟦Q 93:4.3⟧which bestows the favor of God on my faith, not on sacrifices and burnt offerings⟦/Q⟧" [93:4.3]; and to keep the seven commandments and proclaim this good news. [93:4.2-4.4] The second of the seven commandments was, "⟦Q 93:4.8⟧Tu ne douteras pas que la foi soit la seule condition requise pour le salut éternel.⟦/Q⟧." [93:4.8]

No sacrifices were permitted at Salem, and instead of blood sacrifices Melchizedek introduced the sacrament of bread and wine. [93:4.14] But the people of that day were so firmly set in the belief that man is born in debt to the gods that they could hardly grasp the idea of securing God's favor by faith. [93:4.5] He placed all his teaching under the doctrine of one God, the divine Father, and he taught that another Son of God would come, born of a woman, thus preparing the way for Michael. [93:3.6-3.7]

4. The Covenant with Abraham

Melchizedek made a formal covenant with Abraham at Salem. In this covenant "⟦Q 93:6.4⟧God agrees to do everything; man only agrees to believe God's promises and follow his instructions⟦/Q⟧." [93:6.4] Until then it had been believed that salvation could be secured only by sacrifices and offerings, but now the good news was proclaimed that God's favor is to be had by faith. [93:6.4] To commemorate this, Abraham changed his name from Abram to Abraham. [93:6.5]

5. His Departure and Present Status

For several reasons, including the people's tendency to regard him as a demigod, he decided to end his bestowal soon after the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah. [93:8.1] On the third day after his disappearance from Salem he reappeared among his fellow receivers. [93:10.1] For the next nineteen centuries he co-operated with the prophets to preserve the truths of Salem [93:10.4]; after Michael's triumph he became one of the twenty-four directors on Jerusem, and recently he received the title of "⟦Q 93:10.5⟧vicegerent Planetary Prince of Urantia⟦/Q⟧." [93:10.5] The book reports that there have been rulings strongly suggesting that he is destined to take the place of the fallen Caligastia. [93:10.6]

Summary

Machiventa Melchizedek is the emergency Son who volunteered to incarnate in an age when the light of truth was going out; he taught the one God and favor through faith and made a covenant with Abraham, preparing the way for Michael. [93:1.3, 93:3.8, 93:6.4] Today, as vicegerent Planetary Prince of Urantia, he may come to play an important part in the future of this world. [93:10.5, 93:10.11]

q260.question: What relation did Lao-tse, Confucius, and Gautama Siddhartha of the sixth century B.C. have to Melchizedek's Salem teachings, and what did each of them teach?
q260.answer:
The Urantia Book regards the sixth century B.C. as a remarkable century in which the Salem gospel was proclaimed anew through several human teachers. Melchizedek saw the pure doctrines he had taught being endangered by absorption into the older beliefs, and through the co-ordination of spiritual agencies not fully understood even by the planetary supervisors, Urantia witnessed an unprecedented presentation of religious truth. [94:6.1] Lao-tse and Confucius in China and Gautama Siddhartha in India were its representative teachers. [94:6.2, 94:7.1]

1. Lao-tse: Tao and Everlasting Union

Lao-tse "⟦Q 94:6.3⟧built directly upon the concepts of the Salem traditions⟦/Q⟧" [94:6.3] when he declared Tao to be the One First Cause of all creation, and he taught that man's eternal destiny was everlasting union with Tao, Supreme God and Universal King. [94:6.3] He was one of the first to set forth the doctrine of returning good for evil, and he likened true faith to the "⟦Q 94:6.5⟧attitude of a little child⟦/Q⟧." [94:6.4-6.5] His doctrine of nonresistance was later distorted into the belief in doing nothing, but Lao-tse never taught such error. [94:6.7] Present-day popular Taoism has very little in common with the lofty cosmic concepts of this philosopher. [94:6.8]

2. Confucius: Morality and Order

Confucius was a younger contemporary of Lao; he based his doctrines on the long moral traditions of the yellow race and was also somewhat influenced by the traditions of the Salem missionaries. He set a new pace by putting morality in the place of magic, but "⟦Q 94:6.9⟧he built too well; he made a new fetish out of order⟦/Q⟧" [94:6.9] and established a respect for ancestral conduct. His writings became the moral foundation of the culture of almost one third of Urantia's population, but they were somewhat inimical to the investigative spirit of the Chinese. [94:6.11] Mo Ti, who proclaimed a brotherhood based on the love of God, opposed this but was frustrated. [94:6.11]

3. Gautama Siddhartha: A Gospel Close to Salvation by Faith

Gautama decried the practice of seeking salvation through physical suffering, and he fought against the caste system. [94:7.2] At Benares his disciple Bautan passed on to him the traditions of Melchizedek's covenant with Abraham, and although he did not have a clear concept of the Universal Father, he took an advanced stand on salvation through faith and sent his disciples out to proclaim the "good news" of a freely given salvation. [94:7.5] His gospel of universal salvation, free from sacrifice, ritual, and priests, "⟦Q 94:7.7⟧came surprisingly near to being a revival of the Salem gospel⟦/Q⟧" [94:7.7].

But he did not grasp the personality of the One Universal Being, and he failed to present a way to Paradise. [94:7.3] In later years his son and successor wavered from the Salem gospel of divine favor through faith alone, and his dying words in old age were, "⟦Q 94:7.6⟧Work out your own salvation⟦/Q⟧." [94:7.6] In the original teaching, salvation is achieved by human effort apart from divine help, and the book judges it to be "⟦Q 94:8.18⟧the best godless philosophy ever invented by mortal man⟦/Q⟧" and the ideal humanism. [94:8.17-8.18] Its greatest weakness was that it failed to become a religion of unselfish social service. [94:8.19]

4. A Common Fate: Distortion and Deification

Confucius and Lao-tse were eventually raised to the status of gods by their followers. [94:6.12] The book also says that "⟦Q 94:7.8⟧Le bouddhisme moderne ne représente pas plus les enseignements de Gautama Siddharta que le christianisme ne représente les enseignements de Jésus de Nazareth.⟦/Q⟧" [94:7.8], placing it side by side with the fact that modern Christianity is not the original teaching of Jesus.

Summary

The great teachers of the East in the sixth century B.C. each revived in his own way the fading Salem gospel. [94:6.1] Lao-tse taught union with Tao built directly on the Salem traditions, Confucius taught morality and order, and Gautama taught a universal salvation close to the Salem gospel. [94:6.3, 94:6.9, 94:7.7] But because they lacked a clear concept of a personal Universal Father, or because their teachings were later distorted, that light had to await the bestowal of Michael. [94:7.3, 94:6.12]

q261.question: Who was the Egyptian Pharaoh Ikhnaton, why did his monotheistic reform fail, and what did it leave behind?
q261.answer:
The Urantia Book regards Ikhnaton as "⟦Q 95:5.2⟧one of the most remarkable persons in human history⟦/Q⟧." [95:5.2] Since Melchizedek, no human being up to that time had so clearly understood the revealed religion of Salem, and at a time of spiritual depression in Mesopotamia he kept alive in Egypt the doctrine of El Elyon, the One God, thus maintaining the monotheistic channel for the bestowal of Michael. [95:5.2] But because he went too fast and too far ahead, his reform failed in his own day. [95:5.4, 95:5.12]

1. How Did He Come to Know the One God?

As the teachings of Amenemope were fading, a woman of the royal family accepted the teachings of Melchizedek through the influence of a Salemite physician in Egypt, and she persuaded her son Ikhnaton to accept the doctrine of the One God. [95:5.1] The earlier teacher Amenemope had exalted conscience as the supreme standard of right and wrong and taught that God-consciousness is the deciding factor in all conduct. [95:4.1-4.2]

2. Monotheism Hidden under the Guise of the Sun-god

Ikhnaton attempted more systematically than any other king in history to change a whole nation from polytheism to monotheism. He broke with the past, changed his name, abandoned the capital, built a new city, and created a new art and literature. [95:5.4] On the advice of the Salemite physician he sought to approach the worship of the Universal Father by absorbing all the gods into the worship of the sun [95:5.6], and while maintaining the outward worship of Aton he led the people to worship "⟦Q 95:5.7⟧the One God, creator of Aton and supreme Father of all⟦/Q⟧." [95:5.7]

He wrote a book of thirty-one chapters entitled "The One God," but when the priests returned to power they utterly destroyed it; of his one hundred and thirty-seven hymns, twelve are preserved in the Old Testament Book of Psalms. [95:5.7] The supreme word of his religion was "righteousness." [95:5.8]

3. Why Did It Fail?

A reform that went too fast: He built more than could stand after he was gone, and he failed to provide adequately for the material security and prosperity of his people. [95:5.4]

Lack of political genius: It is said that if he had possessed the political sagacity of Moses, he would have changed the history of Occidental religion. [95:5.3, 95:5.5]

Resistance of the priests: The priests secretly kept up their cults and resumed their activities soon after he was gone, and they blamed all of Egypt's troubles on monotheism. [95:5.5]

A concept of God that was too high: His greatest truth, that Aton was the creator of the whole world, was not nationalistic, so it did not raise the morale of the army and handed the priests a weapon. [95:5.9] Moreover only the educated could understand it, and the peasants returned to the worship of Isis and Osiris. [95:5.12]

4. What He Left Behind

His son-in-law returned to the old gods and changed his name to Tutankhamen [95:5.10], but the priests never fully overcame the tide of monotheism and had to combine the gods more and more, and the concept of one God never disappeared from Egypt or the world. [95:5.11] The democracy of salvation and resurrection that he taught finally triumphed. [95:5.13] The aftermath of his work persisted for centuries in Palestine and Greece, and the Hebrew Bedouins sojourning in Egypt perpetuated many of his doctrines in their own religion. [95:5.14-5.15] It was partly in recognition of this exploit that the child Jesus was taken to Egypt, where some of the spiritual successors of Ikhnaton saw him. [95:5.2]

Summary

Ikhnaton was the king who most clearly understood the Salem truth of the One God, and he tried to establish the worship of the Universal Father under the guise of the sun-god. [95:5.2, 95:5.6-5.7] His reform, too fast and too lofty, collapsed in his own day, but his concept of the One God passed on to the Hebrews and the Western world and became part of the background for the bestowal of Michael. [95:5.11, 95:5.14-5.15]

q262.question: How does The Urantia Book use the relation between Moses and Yahweh to explain why the God of the Old Testament is portrayed as jealous and wrathful?
q262.answer:
According to The Urantia Book, Moses knew the lofty concept of El Elyon, the one Most High God, which came from the Melchizedek tradition. But because the ignorant Bedouin slaves could not understand it, he chose the compromise of presenting his new and higher concept of God under the name of their old tribal god, "Yahweh." [96:4.2-4.3] The book explains that the portrayal of the Old Testament God as jealous and wrathful is due to this compromise and to the limited understanding of the people Moses taught. [96:4.7]

1. What Kind of Man Was Moses?

Moses' mother was of the Egyptian royal family, and his father was a Semitic liaison officer. [96:3.1] He was "⟦Q 96:5.1⟧the most important individual world teacher and leader between the times of Machiventa and Jesus⟦/Q⟧" [96:5.1], at once military leader, social organizer, and religious teacher. The Bedouin captives he led had no real concept of God and no hope. [96:3.2-3.3]

2. From El Elyon to Yahweh

Moses had heard the teachings of Machiventa Melchizedek from both his parents; his parents believed in El Shaddai, and his Kenite father-in-law worshiped El Elyon. From all these beliefs he formed an enlarged concept of Deity, and he judged it wise to proclaim it as an expanded concept of the old tribal god Yahweh. [96:4.2] For although he had tried to teach the idea of El Elyon, he was convinced that the people would never comprehend it. [96:4.3] But since Yahweh had long been symbolized by the golden calf of the Bedouin tribes, he was plagued by the awkward predicament of presenting a new idea under the old term. [96:4.3]

3. The Eruption at Sinai and the "Fearful God"

During the third week of their sojourn at the foot of Sinai, Horeb erupted violently, and because of this cataclysm Moses was able to impress upon the people the teaching that God was mighty and terrible, "a devouring fire." [96:4.5] Because he was building a new nation, he nationalized his teachings and spoke of Yahweh as a hard taskmaster, a "jealous God." [96:4.6] Moses also feared to proclaim the mercy of Yahweh, preferring to hold his people in awe through fear of God's justice. [96:5.6] So the Hebrews of this time learned little of the mercy of God and learned of him as a "man of war," a God of battles. [96:5.7]

4. Nevertheless, the Lofty God Moses Pointed To

At the same time Moses sought to enlarge their concept by teaching that Yahweh was the God of the spirits of all flesh and a covenant-keeping God. [96:4.6] He also presented Yahweh as a God of truth and without iniquity, trying to exalt him to the dignity of supreme Deity, but because of the limited understanding of his followers he had to speak of God in the image of man, as having anger, wrath, and vengefulness. [96:4.7] To the assembled leaders he proclaimed that the Lord God is one and there is none beside him. [96:5.5]

5. The Retreat after Moses and the Long Evolution

When Moses died, his lofty concepts rapidly declined, and the people went back to the old ideas of the desert and the worship of the golden calf. [96:5.8, 96:6.1] Yet the book says that the most remarkable feature of Hebrew religious history is precisely the continuous evolution of the concept of Deity, from the primitive god of Mount Horeb up to the teachings of the Isaiahs, who proclaimed God as the loving and merciful Creator Father. [96:4.9] The captivity finally liberated the concept of Yahweh to take on the monotheistic role of God of all peoples. [96:4.8]

Summary

The Old Testament picture of a jealous and wrathful God is not so much God's real character as the result of Moses conveying the lofty concept of El Elyon to an ignorant people under the name of the tribal god Yahweh, putting justice and fear in the foreground. [96:4.3, 96:4.6-4.7, 96:5.6] This concept later grew, through the prophets, into the concept of a loving Father.
