[96:4.9] Therefore when we read the Old Testament, we should also keep in view the fact that the concept of God evolved progressively.

q263.question: How did the Hebrew concept of God develop through the prophets from Samuel to the second Isaiah?
q263.answer:
The Urantia Book credits the spiritual leaders of the Hebrews with the unique achievement of deanthropomorphizing the concept of God without turning it into an abstraction that only philosophers could understand. [97:0.1] From Moses to Malachi the idea of the personality of God grew almost without interruption, and this concept was finally glorified in Jesus' teachings about the Father in heaven. [97:0.2] Each prophet added a new attribute to the earlier concept.

1. Samuel: The Changeless God

Samuel came from a long line of Salem teachers. [97:1.2] His great contribution was the pronouncement that Yahweh was changeless, forever the same embodiment of perfection. At that time Yahweh was thought of as a fitful God, always regretting what he had done, but under Samuel's teaching he began the ascent from the level of a tribal god to the ideal of "⟦Q 97:1.4⟧an all-powerful and changeless Creator and Supervisor of all creation⟦/Q⟧." [97:1.4] Yet Samuel did not get far beyond the tribal concept of a Yahweh concerned chiefly with his chosen people. [97:1.7]

2. Elijah and Elisha: Restoration

Elijah restored to the northern kingdom a concept of God comparable to that of the days of Samuel, but he was so busy tearing down the altars of Baal that he had little opportunity to present advanced concepts. [97:2.1] This was a period of restoration, not of progress, in the concept of Deity. [97:2.3] Elijah transformed the socioeconomic conflict between the Yahwehites and the Baalites over land into a moral and religious issue. [97:3.1, 97:3.6]

3. Amos and Hosea: Justice and Love

Amos was not merely a reformer; he was "⟦Q 97:4.2⟧a discoverer of new concepts of Deity⟦/Q⟧" [97:4.2]. By proclaiming that Yahweh would not tolerate the sins of his people just because they were chosen, he made a direct attack on the egoistic doctrine of the "chosen people," and he proclaimed Yahweh as the God of all nations. [97:4.2, 97:4.4] Hosea revived Moses' concept of a God of love, preaching forgiveness through repentance, not by sacrifice. [97:4.5] If Amos awakened the national conscience, Hosea sounded the first notes of the chord of divine compassion and loving-kindness. [97:4.7]

4. The First Isaiah, Micah, and Jeremiah: Expansion and Internationalization

The first Isaiah preached the eternal nature of God, his infinite wisdom, and his unchanging reliability. [97:5.2] Micah and Obadiah fearlessly attacked the whole priest-ridden system of ritual and sacrifice. [97:5.4] Jeremiah declared that Yahweh was not on the side of the Hebrews in their military struggles but was God of all the earth and of all nations, and his teaching was "⟦Q 97:6.2⟧the crescendo of the rising wave of the internationalization of the God of Israel⟦/Q⟧" [97:6.2].

5. The Second Isaiah: The Loving Universal Father

The priests of the captivity, out of resentment over their lost national deity, inflated their history [97:7.1], but the young prophet, the second Isaiah, greatly curbed their influence. [97:7.4] "⟦Q 97:7.5⟧No prophet or religious teacher from Machiventa to the time of Jesus attained the high concept of God that Isaiah the second proclaimed during these days of the captivity⟦/Q⟧." [97:7.5] He eclipsed the nationalistic Yahweh and portrayed a God embracing universal justice, divine mercy, and eternal righteousness; he "⟦Q 97:7.13⟧portrayed the all-powerful Creator as the all-loving Father⟦/Q⟧." [97:7.13] The book says that at last Machiventa Melchizedek beheld human teachers proclaiming a real God. [97:7.6]

Summary

The Hebrew concept of God grew from Samuel's 'changeless God,' through Amos's 'God of justice who judges all nations fairly,' Hosea's 'God of love and mercy,' and Jeremiah's 'God of all nations,' to the second Isaiah's 'Universal Father who loves all.' [97:1.4, 97:4.2-4.5, 97:6.2, 97:7.13] This long evolution became the foundation for receiving Jesus' teaching about the Father in heaven. [97:0.2]

q264.question: Christianity and Mithraism are said to resemble each other in many ways. How does The Urantia Book explain the elements from which present-day Christianity was formed?
q264.answer:
The Urantia Book explains that Christianity was formed around the person of Jesus of Nazareth, but that as a system of belief it was made up of a combination of seven elements: the teachings of Melchizedek, Hebrew theology, Zoroastrianism, the mystery cults such as Mithraism, the life of Jesus, the viewpoint of Paul, and Greek philosophy. [98:7.2-7.10] In particular, during the three centuries after Christ, Christianity competed with Mithraism and came to resemble it greatly in outward form and ceremony. [98:6.3]

1. The Mystery Cults and Mithraism

Many people in the Greco-Roman world had lost their primitive family and national religions and could not grasp Greek philosophy, so they turned to the emotional mystery cults of Egypt and the Levant. [98:4.1] The Phrygian and Egyptian mysteries taught that a divine son had died and been raised again, and that the initiates shared in the immortality of that god. [98:4.6] These cults finally gave way to the greatest of the mystery cults, the worship of Mithras, which spread throughout the empire by way of the Roman legions. [98:5.1] It was chiefly through the Mithraic cult that the religion of Zoroaster influenced Christianity. [98:5.2]

2. Familiar Elements within Mithraism

The story of Mithras included a flood from which one man escaped in a boat, and a last supper with the sun-god before his ascension to heaven. [98:5.3] Its devotees held weekly services on the day of the sun-god, and the most elaborate ceremony was the annual festival of Mithras on December twenty-fifth. They believed that partaking of the sacrament assured eternal life, and that at the end of the world Mithras would call forth the dead for the last judgment. [98:5.4]

3. The Resemblances and the Decisive Difference between the Two Religions

In both religions the places of worship were mostly underground, and both had altars depicting the sufferings of a savior who had brought salvation to a sin-cursed human race. [98:6.3] The Mithraic custom of dipping the fingers in holy water passed into the Christian churches in the vicinity of Rome, and both religions employed baptism and partook of the sacrament of bread and wine. [98:6.4]

The differences were clear. The characters of Mithras and Jesus were different, and Mithraism encouraged militarism while Christianity was ultrapacific. And the deciding factor in the competition was "⟦Q 98:6.4⟧the admission of women into the full fellowship of the Christian faith⟦/Q⟧." [98:6.4] Mithraism at first was a religion for men only. [98:5.5]

4. The Seven Elements That Made Up Christianity

The book sums up the elements of Christianity as follows.

The teachings of Melchizedek: the basic factor in all the religions of East and West during the past four thousand years. [98:7.4]

The Hebrew heritage: morals, ethics, theology, and belief in Providence and the supreme Yahweh. [98:7.5]

Zoroastrianism: the concept of the cosmic struggle between good and evil, which through contact with Mithraism strongly influenced the structure of doctrine and cosmology. [98:7.6]

The mystery cults: even the legends of the birth of Jesus became tainted with the Roman version of the birth of Mithras, said to have been witnessed only by gift-bearing shepherds. [98:7.7]

The life of Jesus: the historical life of Joshua ben Joseph and the reality of the glorified Christ. [98:7.8]

The viewpoint of Paul: in Tarsus during his youth Mithraism was dominant, and he never imagined that his letters would later be regarded as "⟦Q 98:7.9⟧the word of God⟦/Q⟧." [98:7.9]

Greek philosophy: combined with Pauline theology, it forms the basis of European ethics to this day. [98:7.10]

In the end, Greek philosophy supplied the concepts of ethical value; Mithraism, the ritual of worship observance; and Christianity, the technique for the conservation of moral and social values. [98:6.5]

5. The Religion of Jesus and the Religion about Jesus

The book stresses that the Creator Son came not to appease an angry God but to lead all mankind to the recognition of the Father's love and of sonship with God. [98:7.1] Christianity has glorified Jesus as the Messiah "⟦Q 98:7.11⟧but has largely forgotten the Master's personal gospel: the Fatherhood of God and the universal brotherhood of all men⟦/Q⟧." [98:7.11]

Summary

Present-day Christianity is a religion that puts Jesus at its center while combining elements from Melchizedek, the Hebrews, Zoroaster, Mithraism, Paul, and Greek philosophy, and it closely resembles Mithraism in outward forms such as the sacrament, baptism, holy water, and the savior's altar. [98:6.3-6.4, 98:7.3-7.10] The Urantia Book urges us to know this history while recovering the gospel of Jesus himself that lies hidden within it: the Fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man. [98:7.11]
